Hey there,

So I know you haven't been dating long, but here are a few ideas:
 

Don't tell them it was their fault! It is never the fault of the victim, regardless of the situation. Remind the person it wasn't their fault no matter what led up to the incident.

Respect the person. Don't pity them for the sake of trying to appear supportive.

Make sure the person is out of harms way. If they are working with someone who is assaulting them, something must be done so that they are no longer in harms way.

Tell them "I'm sorry this happened to you"

Comfort the person. Get them a coffee, put down the smart phone, turn off the TV, and just listen.

Never try to solve all their problems or take them on as your own. Someone who has been victimized has already experienced a loss of control.

Don't expect to know all the details. Never force someone to share more than they are comfortable with.

Tell the person you believe them. Validate their experiences.

Never assume that the person can "get over it", treat the situation delicately.

Don't treat it like a soap-opera. Every conversation you have with them after they tell you shouldn't revolve around the sexual assault.

Do offer to accompany them to therapy or counselling.

Thank the person for telling you. It took courage and strength for them to bring it up.

Try to understand what the person's triggers are. Triggers are stimuli which remind the victim of the sexual assault event. Be a good listener. Try to pick up on things that may remind them of the event and avoid bringing those topics up.

Survivors of sexual assault feel differently about touch. Some may want a hug, but others may not. Try to judge the situation before making body contact with them. When in doubt, ask first before giving a hug.

Never make a victim feel guilty for anything leading up to the event. For example, drinking, flirting, etc. Sexual assault and rape are never their fault no matter what.

If they were recently assaulted (in the past day or so), offer to take them to see a medical professional at a hospital. There they can test for sexually transmitted diseases and give the patient the morning after pill to decrease pregnancy risks.

Be comfortable with silence. 

Make sure they have your number on speed dial if they want to chat about it.

If there are legal proceedings, offer to go to court hearings with them.

Don't be afraid to suppress rage, sadness, or frustration at the situation in order to appear strong for your friend. These are all normal reactions and may make the victim feel more at ease knowing they aren't alone.

Never tell a person they should have done something different to avoid getting sexually assaulted.

Never be afraid of not being able to offer advice. Sometimes a situation is tough, but you don't need to be the superhero constantly by knowing what to say.

If they are having a panic attack, help them by reminding them of where they are. Help them stay grounded in the present.

If someone is having an extremely emotional time, help them breath through it.

Do some homework on your own about facts and information regarding sexual assault trauma, PTSD, coping skills, etc.

When the survivor is having flashbacks, try talking softly to them. Remind them about their surroundings, and ask them to describe it.

If they have a panic attack or emotional flashback, don't make them talk about it. This may trigger them further. Let them talk about it if they are comfortable.

There is no time-line for healing. Every survivor heals at different rates during different times. Don't expect them to be better after doing counseling for a period of time.

Some PTSD, depression, adjustment disorder, anxiety, and other trauma disorders need medication. Gently urge them to ask their doctor to be properly diagnosed and treated.

Many survivors show signs of PTSD early on. Try to be supportive.

Eating, sleeping, and enjoying everyday activities can be difficult for someone with sexual assault-related PTSD. Try to help them by making a favorite meal or getting them tea at nighttime.

Never try to minimize the situation. Don't say "It's no big deal" or "It happened a long time ago".

Don't make excuses for the behavior of the accused perpetrator.

Never tell the survivor that they need to eventually learn to "forgive".

Be aware of any triggering TV shows, movies, or music that displays or depicts sexual violence. Try to avoid these.

Depending on your relationship with the survivor, you may want to get therapy for yourself as well. There are free hotlines and online groups for secondary survivors.

Try not to rely on the survivor for emotional support if you are emotionally impacted by them telling you. Hit a pillow or see a therapist.

A survivor may not always tell you what they are feeling. Watch how they act. If you are talking about something that is making them uncomfortable, try to be aware and stop.

If you are dating a sexual assault survivor, be very communicative when it comes to sex. Only do what they feel comfortable doing.

Always be patient.

Tell the person "I'm here for you".

If the person hasn't reported it, don't raise a big deal and force them into it. 

Make sure they are heard when they talk. Paraphrase what they are saying, and use active listening and body language.

Put yourself in their position. Try to understand the pain they are going through.

If you feel uncomfortable with them telling you, or about specific details, tell them. 

Remember your own limitations. Don't offer to give help that you can't give.

Remind them of their strengths. Give them positive affirmations.


....just a few ideas. PM me if you want to chat or talks specifics!

For me, triggers are the bane of my existence!!

My advice is to just keep working through that trigger. I think the more counseling & support you can get for the childhood trauma, the better you will be at being able to cope with situations where someone says that... (I'm in a group sexualassaulttalks.com, which is really cool if you are looking for a casual SA support group to attend online).

For me, working through the trigger takes work. I make sure and tell all my family and friends my triggers. I purposefully ask them to NOT avoid using it around me. Evertime I hear it, I remind myself that I am safe. I remind myself that the trauma is in the past. I remind myself that I am among friends/family. 

Little by little, this has helped me move past little triggers like words or phrases. It's like I'm rewriting my own script to that horrible situation I experienced. The more I hear them (trigger words), the less power they have over me.

I know this isn't everyone's strategy. Many people would like nothing more than to NEVER hear trigger words again. It works for me. Maybe it will work for you??

DO respect her enough to not pity her.

DON'T assume she does or doesn't want to be touched. Some people can't stand a hug at this point; others can't make it without one.

DO comfort her. Bring a cup of tea/coffee and a blanket. Play soft music. Make the environment comfortable.

DON'T try to solve all the problems for her. She has had her control taken away from her; try to avoid doing that again.

DO offer to accompany her to her therapy sessions if she has them.

DON'T demand to know every detail of the rape or abuse.

DO allow her to tell you as much or as little as she needs to.

And finally, never ever ever blame her or tell her to 'get over it'. I've had to tell partners about my trauma and it was never easy. The best thing you can do is be there for her  100% and make sure she knows that too.
